item.title: Libya's secret executions: Why now?
item.description:
Libya's secret executions: Why now?

At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya after being sentenced to death in secret military trials by the Libyan Armed Forces, under commander Khalifa Haftar, for the first time since 2010.

Human Rights Watch's Ahmed Benchemsi tells Mathilda Mallinson on MEE Live that the executions have been able to go ahead now due to lack of accountability against actors in the region and international actors with interests in Libyan factions.

At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya after being sentenced to death in secret military trials by the Libyan Armed Forces, under commander Khalifa Haftar.

item.title: Qatar's prime minister calls Netanyahu 'war criminal', says Doha will continue diplomacy efforts in region
item.description:
Qatar's prime minister calls Netanyahu 'war criminal', says Doha will continue diplomacy efforts in region

Qatar's prime minister accused his Israeli counterpart, Benjamin Netanyahu, of being a "war criminal", and stressed that Doha would continue its mediation efforts despite escalating tensions in the region. 

During an interview with Piers Morgan, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani - who is also Qatar's foreign minister - was asked whether he considered Netanyahu a war criminal. 

Sheikh Mohammad responded by saying: "Of course. What’s been committed in Gaza is war crimes, and whoever is responsible for this is a war criminal."

"Hospitals have been targeted, schools have been targeted. Whatever the justifications and the arguments, nothing is justifying this," he added.

He also brought up Israel's attack on Qatar in early September of last year, when it targeted Hamas officials while Doha was engaged in mediation efforts.

"We were attacked by Israel while we were mediating," he said. "Netanyahu has crossed the line like he has crossed other lines before that."

 Despite escalating regional tensions, Sheikh Mohammed indicated Qatar's readiness in ongoing diplomacy and mediation efforts.

"We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians," he said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis
item.description:
Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis

Saudi Arabia appears to be mending fences with the UAE in an effort to push back a Houthi military offensive in Yemen that threatens the kingdom’s Red Sea oil export corridor and has seen drones strike Riyadh.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman hosted the UAE’s Vice President, Mansour Bin Zayed, in Riyadh on Tuesday, marking the kingdom's most prominent effort yet to reconcile with the UAE after clashing over Sudan, Yemen, and Somaliland.

“The Houthis are bringing Saudi Arabia and the UAE closer together,” Anna Jacobs, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told Middle East Eye.

The two neighbours have been discussing how to collaborate on Yemen for months, western and Arab officials tell MEE, but the talks have been moving slowly.

Read more: Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis

item.title: Saudi official denies reports of meeting taking place with Israeli officials
item.description:
Saudi official denies reports of meeting taking place with Israeli officials

A senior Saudi official on Wednesday has denied reports of a meeting taking place between representatives from Saudi Arabia and Israeli officials. 

On Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Abu Dhabi and met UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan -  a meeting that was confirmed by both Israeli and Emirati officials.

According to Israeli media reports, representatives from Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Libya, Qatar and Morocco were also present at the meeting.

item.title: Committee on Exercise of Inalienable Rights of Palestinian People meets with UN's Guterres
item.description:
Committee on Exercise of Inalienable Rights of Palestinian People meets with UN's Guterres

The Bureau of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People held a meeting on Tuesday with United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres.

Chair of the Committee and Permanent Representative of Senegal to the UN Cheikh Niang praised the Secretary-General’s principled and strong positions in defending the rights of the Palestinian people and expressed the Committee’s gratitude for his support in fulfilling its mandate in accordance with the relevant General Assembly resolution.

item.title: US Treasury Secretary says economic action against Iran to continue
item.description:
US Treasury Secretary says economic action against Iran to continue

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that the economic measures against Iran will continue, targeting those providing financial support to Iran.

“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” Bessent said.

“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers,” he added.

Meanwhile, US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott highlighted on Tuesday a $15m reward offered by the US government for information that disrupts the financial mechanisms of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

item.title: Palestinian boy shot by Israeli gunfire during raid on al-Fara'a refugee camp
item.description:
Palestinian boy shot by Israeli gunfire during raid on al-Fara'a refugee camp

A Palestinian boy was injured on Tuesday by Israeli forces’ live gunfire during a raid on al-Fara'a refugee camp, south of Tubas in the occupied West Bank, Wafa news reported.

Red Crescent sources told Wafa that their crews treated a boy who sustained a gunshot wound to the hand.

item.title: Yemeni government forces say they conducted 414 strikes on Houthis in last 24 hours
item.description:
Yemeni government forces say they conducted 414 strikes on Houthis in last 24 hours

Yemen’s armed forces spokesman Majid al-Nuzaili said on Tuesday that Yemeni government forces carried out 414 “precision strikes” targeting Houthi positions over the past 24 hours.

In a statement, al-Nuzaili said the operations had been a success in “neutralising numerous Houthi personnel and assets”.

The Houthi-affiliated al-Masirah news channel reported numerous attacks in Yemen’s Taiz, Hodeidah and Sa’dah governorates in recent hours, which they said were carried out by Saudi forces.

item.title: UAE condemns storming of Al-Aqsa Mosque by Israeli settlers
item.description:
UAE condemns storming of Al-Aqsa Mosque by Israeli settlers

The UAE foreign ministry issued a statement on Tuesday condemning the storming of Al-Aqsa Mosque by Israeli settlers, led by far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Ben-Gvir joined hundreds of Israeli settlers who stormed the courtyards of Al-Aqsa Mosque complex on Monday and joined settlers in storming the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron on Tuesday.

The UAE called the storming of Al-Aqsa a “provocative escalation and an unacceptable extremist act”.

item.title: Manchester City chief claims 'conspiracy' as UAE-owned club found guilty of financial violations charges
item.description:
Manchester City chief claims 'conspiracy' as UAE-owned club found guilty of financial violations charges

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 20:29
The football club now has until Friday to appeal the independent commission's findings
Manchester City striker Erling Haaland is pictured during the Fifa Club World Cup 2025 round of 16 football match between his team and Saudi Arabia's Al Hilal, at the Camping World stadium in Orlando, Florida, on 30 June 2025 (Patricia De Melo/AFP)
Off

An independent commission on Tuesday revealed that Manchester City Football Club has been found guilty on all 115 charges related to financial rules violations.

The club engaged in "sham" commercial contracts to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than $1bn, the findings showed. 

"The Club’s financial statements had not been prepared and audited in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory principles," the commission wrote. 

It was "reckless" and "acted other than with utmost good faith", it added. 

In a video sent to staff and players and obtained by Sky Sports News, City's chief executive, Ferran Soriano, called the investigation a "Premier League conspiracy theory". 

The Premier League charged City in 2023 after an investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018. 

It was accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules. 

“This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in [our] history," the Premier League said in a statement on Tuesday.

"[It] vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently," the statement added. 

"It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."

While the sanctions are yet to be decided, City is looking at a points deduction serious enough to relegate the team to a lower league division as well as significant fines.

Leaked documents

The club is owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, deputy prime minister and vice president of the UAE, who bought the club in September 2008 for $265m. 

Under Sheikh Mansour's ownership, City has become the dominant force in English football. 

Manchester United co-owner slammed for claiming UK 'colonised' by migrants
Read More »

It has won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups, and one Champions League in the past 15 years. 

Investigations into City’s financial breaches began after German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents in 2018.

Emails purportedly exchanged between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from Abu Dhabi state-controlled airline Etihad and telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.

ADUG is a prominent investor in urban regeneration.

During his tenure as Manchester mayor, current UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised City’s owners and the funding they put into the east of the city.

Burnham held his first phone call with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Sheikh Mansour’s brother, in late July, as he seeks to broaden the UK’s investment appeal to wealthy allies like the UAE.

item.title: Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis
item.description:
Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 20:13
Saudi Arabia's warm welcome for UAE's vice president could foreshadow military cooperation against Houthis, but differences persist
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (R) and UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan meeting in Riyadh on 29 September 2026 (Saudi Press Agency/AFP)
Off

Saudi Arabia appears to be mending fences with the UAE in an effort to push back a Houthi military offensive in Yemen that threatens the kingdom’s Red Sea oil export corridor and has seen drones strike Riyadh.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman hosted the UAE’s Vice President, Mansour Bin Zayed, in Riyadh on Tuesday, marking the kingdom's most prominent effort yet to reconcile with the UAE after clashing over Sudan, Yemen, and Somaliland.

“The Houthis are bringing Saudi Arabia and the UAE closer together,” Anna Jacobs, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told Middle East Eye.

The two neighbours have been discussing how to collaborate on Yemen for months, western and Arab officials tell MEE, but the talks have been moving slowly.

The UAE wanted a public signal from Saudi Arabia that it had put its spat behind it, along with concessions to Abu Dhabi’s allies on the ground in Yemen, the Western official told MEE. In July, Saudi Arabia shared a casual photograph of Mansour and Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Khaled bin Salman, together, but the location and time of the meeting were not disclosed.

The Houthis' lightning offensive in September down the Red Sea coast was the catalyst for a bigger meeting, experts say.

Mansour, the brother of UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed, was greeted at the airport by Khaled Bin Salman, the crown prince’s brother, whom MEE revealed was tapped by the crown prince in February to mend the rift.

Following Mansour’s visit, the UAE dispatched two Boeing planes with officials to Riyadh in order to coordinate over Yemen, two western officials familiar with the matter told MEE.

Saudi crown prince sent complaint letter to UAE 'spy sheikh' about Yemen, Sudan
Read More »

Joshua Yaphe, a senior fellow at the Center for the National Interest, and former lead analyst on the Arabian Gulf at the State Department’s intelligence bureau, told MEE the symbolism of Mansour’s visit was important to Abu Dhabi.

“Yemen is going downhill fast, and everybody knows it. The Emiratis know the Saudis are in a worrisome position and they don’t want to see the Saudis flat-out fail, so they are coming in on a white horse, saying, ‘we can help you, if you are nice to us’,” he said.

Saudi Arabia was rebuffed by the US when it sought military assistance against the Houthis earlier this month, and its defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan has not kicked in over the escalation. 

Western officials who work with Saudi Arabia on military operations in Yemen breathed a sigh of relief that Mansour’s visit was successful.

A former US official told MEE that Riyadh’s move could help unlock more cooperation from the Trump administration, which has wanted the Gulf spat resolved. 

Can the UAE turn the tide in Yemen?

Saudi Arabia and the UAE joined forces in 2015 to fight the Houthis after they conquered the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, and a wide swath of the northeast.

The UAE dispatched ground forces in addition to training and arming Yemeni factions that were widely considered to be the most effective at fighting. In 2017, forces backed by the UAE ousted the Houthis from the Red Sea coast and rallied to prevent the group, which is armed by Iran, from taking the port city of Aden.

But Saudi Arabia clashed with the UAE over its support for the Southern Transitional Council, a group that wants to revive an independent Yemeni state in the south. Northern Yemen was ravaged by a bloody civil war in the 1960s, while southern Yemen became an independent Marxist state until its unification with the north in 1990.

In December 2025, Saudi Arabia bombed UAE weapons shipments to the STC and launched a military offensive against the group after it swept across much of the country’s south. The UAE announced its withdrawal from Yemen.

'The UAE was the most effective part of the military coalition'

- Kristian Ulrichsen, Baker Institute

One diplomat in the region told MEE that the UAE has asked Saudi Arabia to open space for the STC after it was disbanded in January. 

The UAE also wants Saudi Arabia to ban Islah, Yemen’s main Sunni Islamist party, which is part of Yemen's international government. The UAE has been lobbying the US to label the party a terrorist organisation.

“The Emirates are not going to get what they want from the Saudis: a disavowal of Islah and an acceptance of the STC,” Yaphe told MEE. “[But] the Saudis might tell the Yemeni government to play nicer with the STC in a cabinet reshuffle.”

“The bigger question is, even if the Emiratis put a ton of support behind the Yemeni government, can that turn the tide of the war? In the past, they were able to salvage things, but what’s their capacity now?” Yaphe said.

The UAE’s Yemeni allies include the STC's Security Belt Forces, the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces (NRF). The latter is commanded by Tarik Saleh, the nephew of Yemen’s former president who aligned with the Houthis before being killed by them. The NRF was in control of Yemen’s southern Red Sea coastline before the Houthis defeated them.

Despite its withdrawal from Yemen earlier this year, experts say the UAE has strong leverage over these southern Yemeni factions, in addition to skilled Emirati officers and special forces who effectively commanded troops on the ground a decade ago against the Houthis. 

“This meeting was all about Yemen,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a Gulf expert and fellow at the Baker Institute, told MEE. “The Saudis are preparing to make a significant move against the Houthis and want to make sure the anti-Houthi coalition is not as fragmented as it’s been.”

“The UAE can play a significant role even without getting involved militarily by using their influence on the STC and Tarek Saleh. The UAE was the most effective part of the military coalition,” he added.

Structural competition?

Saudi Arabia has been launching strikes on the Houthis, but it has also faced drone and missile attacks. Riyadh airport was bombed earlier this month, and the East-West Pipeline was temporarily disabled by an attack the kingdom said emanated from Iraq. Shia militias in Iraq have coordinated with the Houthis.

A former US official told MEE that Saudi Arabia could ask for Emirati assistance on air defence.

'The Emiratis know the Saudis are in a worrisome position so they are coming in on a white horse'

- Joshua Yaphe, Center for the National

The Trump administration has been trying to push its Gulf allies, particularly the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, to coordinate more.

Saudi Arabia's coordination with the UAE could also lead to more cooperation with Israel, which deployed an iron-dome battery in the UAE during the height of fighting with Iran. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the UAE on Sunday. 

While some Gulf officials are optimistic about the chances of Saudi Arabia and the UAE resuming cooperation in Yemen, experts caution that they remain far apart on key files.

For example, Saudi Arabia condemned, in January, Israel’s recognition of Somaliland across the Gulf of Aden. The UAE owns a commercial port in Berbera and has a military base there. 

Saudi Arabia and the UAE also support opposing sides in Sudan’s civil war.

In addition to meeting Mansour on Tuesday, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had a phone call with Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the chief of Sudan's military that Saudi Arabia supports against the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces militia. The UAE may look for concessions from Saudi Arabia on Sudan and Somaliland, analysts say.

Still, Jacobs at the Arab Gulf States Institute said a return to Saudi Arabian and UAE dialogue could de-escalate tensions in the Red Sea.

“This could have a positive implication for the wider Red Sea because of the two’s proxy competition,” she told MEE. “The question is whether this can be sustained at a high level because their competition is structural.”

Trump says he does not know if Iran is going to 'give up yet'

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Iran is doing "very poorly," adding that he does not know if Iran is going to "give up yet" regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran, in comments delivered to reporters outside the White House following a meeting with AI executives.

item.title: IRGC issues open letter urging US voters to 'wrest control back from corrupt politicians'
item.description:
IRGC issues open letter urging US voters to 'wrest control back from corrupt politicians'

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) released on Tuesday an open letter addressed to US voters, calling on them to "wake up" and "wrest control back from corrupt politicians".

In a lengthy open letter, the IRGC directly appealed to American voters, telling them, "you are the ones who empower, with your votes, the government and allow it to do what it does".

"The United States of America is a great nation. To allow vulgar and immoral individuals to continue steering your politics and policies will only further humiliate and undermine the US," the letter continued, urging the American public to "take back control".

This comes ahead of the US midterm elections at a time when Trump's popularity is at an all-time low.

item.title: Yemeni government forces claim strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s al-Wazi’yah
item.description:
Yemeni government forces claim strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s al-Wazi’yah

Yemen’s armed forces spokesman Majid al-Nuzaili said in a statement on Tuesday that Yemeni government forces carried out eight strikes on Houthi positions in the al-Wazi’yah district of the Taiz governorate, targeting Houthi vehicles, equipment and personnel.

This comes after Yemen's army warned civilians to stay away from sites used by the Houthis for military activities, saying they consider them to be legitimate targets.

item.title: Netanyahu says he filed libel lawsuits over October 7 warning allegations
item.description:
Netanyahu says he filed libel lawsuits over October 7 warning allegations

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that he filed defamation lawsuits against allegations that he had received warnings ahead of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. 

In a post on X, the prime minister called the claims "false slanders", writing that "it is no coincidence that these lies are being spread now, on the eve of elections, by political rivals and hostile foreign actors" who want to topple his "right-wing government" and "install a left-wing-Arab parties government" which seeks to "establish a Palestinian state".

Earlier this month, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu about a possible attack by Hamas 10 days before the events of 7 October 2023.

item.title: Yemen government forces warn all sites used by Houthis legitimate targets
item.description:
Yemen government forces warn all sites used by Houthis legitimate targets

Yemen’s Armed Forces issued a statement warning civilians to stay away from sites used by the Houthis for military activities.

In a statement, the army said they consider the sites to be legitimate targets, adding that any action against them would be carried out in accordance with international humanitarian law.

Spokesperson Brigadier-General Majed al-Nazili said that the army is monitoring and tracking Houthi military movements and activities across various fronts.

item.title: Hundreds of families stranded inside their vehicles at checkpoint near Ramallah
item.description:
Hundreds of families stranded inside their vehicles at checkpoint near Ramallah

Hundreds of Palestinian families have been stranded inside their vehicles for hours at the Atara checkpoint, north of Ramallah, due to tightened Israeli restrictions, Wafa news reported on Tuesday.

Israeli forces sealed off the permanently staffed checkpoint, with large numbers of vehicles backed up and long queues stretching for considerable distances.

Israeli soldiers also closed the Ein Sinya checkpoint, north of Ramallah, forcing Palestinians to wait for hours in their vehicles, according to Wafa news.
